results.name: singleton_distance_gradient
results.description: Among single-example sets, yes rate for targets within 10 of the example (excluding the example itself) minus yes rate for targets more than 30 away; observed below null means people generalise less locally (flatter similarity gradient) than the model's interval mechanism predicts, above null means a steeper gradient.
results.code:
# name: singleton_distance_gradient
# description: Among single-example sets, yes rate for targets within 10 of the example (excluding the example itself) minus yes rate for targets more than 30 away; observed below null means people generalise less locally (flatter similarity gradient) than the model's interval mechanism predicts, above null means a steeper gradient.
def test_statistic(df):
    s = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    single = ~s.str.contains(",")
    if single.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    x = pd.to_numeric(s[single], errors="coerce").to_numpy()
    t = df.loc[single, "target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    r = df.loc[single, "rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    dist = np.abs(t - x)
    near = (dist > 0) & (dist <= 10)
    far = dist > 30
    a = r[near].mean() if near.any() else 0.0
    b = r[far].mean() if far.any() else 0.0
    return float(a - b)

results.name: within_pair_response_variance
results.description: Mean over repeated (set, target) pairs of the within-pair Bernoulli variance p(1-p) of yes responses; observed above null means human answers to the same item are more mixed (less all-or-none) than the model's predicted probabilities, below null means humans are more unanimous than the model.

results.name: example_as_target_yes_rate
results.description: Yes rate on trials where the target is one of the set's own examples; observed below null means people reject shown examples more often than the model (which treats examples as near-certain members) predicts.

results.name: odd_set_odd_target_gap
results.description: Among sets of 2+ examples that are all odd but not all prime, yes rate on odd non-example targets minus yes rate on even targets; observed above null means people generalise "odd numbers" more strongly than the model (whose odd cost suppresses it), below null means weaker.
results.code:
# name: odd_set_odd_target_gap
# description: Among sets of 2+ examples that are all odd but not all prime, yes rate on odd non-example targets minus yes rate on even targets; observed above null means people generalise "odd numbers" more strongly than the model (whose odd cost suppresses it), below null means weaker.
def test_statistic(df):
    parts = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True)
    ex = parts.apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    valid = ~np.isnan(ex)
    n = valid.sum(axis=1)
    exi = np.where(valid, ex, 1).astype(int)
    allodd = np.where(valid, exi % 2 == 1, True).all(axis=1)
    primes = np.array([k > 1 and all(k % d for d in range(2, int(k ** 0.5) + 1)) for k in range(101)])
    allprime = np.where(valid, primes[np.clip(exi, 0, 100)], True).all(axis=1)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    isex = (ex == t[:, None]).any(axis=1)
    sel = (n >= 2) & allodd & ~allprime & ~isex
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    o = sel & (t % 2 == 1)
    e = sel & (t % 2 == 0)
    if o.sum() == 0 or e.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[o].mean() - r[e].mean())

results.name: unstructured_set_in_range_yes
results.description: Among 3-4 example sets with no shared parity, final digit or times table (2..12), yes rate on non-example targets inside the set's [min,max] range minus yes rate on targets outside it; observed below null means people treat wide "random-looking" sets less as a contiguous range than the model's interval hypotheses predict, above null means more.
results.code:
# name: unstructured_set_in_range_yes
# description: Among 3-4 example sets with no shared parity, final digit or times table (2..12), yes rate on non-example targets inside the set's [min,max] range minus yes rate on targets outside it; observed below null means people treat wide "random-looking" sets less as a contiguous range than the model's interval hypotheses predict, above null means more.
def test_statistic(df):
    parts = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True)
    ex = parts.apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    valid = ~np.isnan(ex)
    n = valid.sum(axis=1)
    exi = np.where(valid, ex, 0).astype(int)
    shared = np.zeros(len(df), dtype=bool)
    for m in range(2, 13):
        shared |= np.where(valid, exi % m == 0, True).all(axis=1)
    shared |= np.where(valid, exi % 2 == 1, True).all(axis=1)
    last = np.where(valid, exi % 10, -1)
    shared |= np.where(valid, last == last[:, :1], True).all(axis=1)
    lo = np.nanmin(ex, axis=1)
    hi = np.nanmax(ex, axis=1)
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    isex = (ex == t[:, None]).any(axis=1)
    sel = (n >= 3) & ~shared & ~isex
    inside = sel & (t >= lo) & (t <= hi)
    outside = sel & ((t < lo) | (t > hi))
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    if inside.sum() == 0 or outside.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[inside].mean() - r[outside].mean())

results.name: shared_final_digit_generalisation
results.description: Among sets of 2+ examples that all share one final digit d, yes rate on non-example targets ending in d minus yes rate on other targets; observed below null means people generalise the "ends in d" rule less than the model's final-digit discount predicts, above null means more.
results.code:
# name: shared_final_digit_generalisation
# description: Among sets of 2+ examples that all share one final digit d, yes rate on non-example targets ending in d minus yes rate on other targets; observed below null means people generalise the "ends in d" rule less than the model's final-digit discount predicts, above null means more.
def test_statistic(df):
    parts = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True)
    ex = parts.apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    valid = ~np.isnan(ex)
    n = valid.sum(axis=1)
    last = np.where(valid, np.nan_to_num(ex) % 10, np.nan)
    first = last[:, 0]
    same = np.where(valid, last == first[:, None], True).all(axis=1)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    isex = (ex == t[:, None]).any(axis=1)
    sel = (n >= 2) & same & ~isex
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    m = sel & (t % 10 == first)
    o = sel & (t % 10 != first)
    if m.sum() == 0 or o.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[m].mean() - r[o].mean())

results.name: yes_rate_trial_slope
results.description: OLS slope of yes response on trial_index (per 100 trials) across all trials; observed below null means people say yes less as the session goes on (a fatigue/criterion drift the stationary model cannot produce), above null means rising yes rate.

results.name: times_table_rule_sharpness
results.description: Among sets of 2+ examples that are all multiples of some m in 3,4,6,7,8,9,11,12 (largest such m; multiples of 5/10 excluded), yes rate on non-example multiples of m minus yes rate on non-multiples; observed below null means people endorse the shared times table less sharply than the model (e.g. rejecting multiples of 8 after 8,64), above null means more sharply.
results.code:
# name: times_table_rule_sharpness
# description: Among sets of 2+ examples that are all multiples of some m in 3,4,6,7,8,9,11,12 (largest such m; multiples of 5/10 excluded), yes rate on non-example multiples of m minus yes rate on non-multiples; observed below null means people endorse the shared times table less sharply than the model (e.g. rejecting multiples of 8 after 8,64), above null means more sharply.
def test_statistic(df):
    parts = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True)
    ex = parts.apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    valid = ~np.isnan(ex)
    n = valid.sum(axis=1)
    exi = np.where(valid, ex, 0).astype(int)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    mm = np.zeros(len(df), dtype=int)
    for m in [3, 4, 6, 7, 8, 9, 11, 12]:
        ok = (np.where(valid, exi % m == 0, True)).all(axis=1)
        mm = np.where(ok, m, mm)
    five = (np.where(valid, exi % 5 == 0, True)).all(axis=1)
    isex = (ex == t[:, None]).any(axis=1)
    sel = (n >= 2) & (mm > 0) & ~five & ~isex
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    mult = sel & (t % np.maximum(mm, 1) == 0)
    non = sel & (t % np.maximum(mm, 1) != 0)
    if mult.sum() == 0 or non.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[mult].mean() - r[non].mean())
